name: Dopamine / porn avoidance

card.summary: Abstaining from porn, masturbation or other stimulation to 'reset' dopamine, popular in self-improvement circles; claimed benefits lack supporting evidence per researchers.
card.note: Researchers say prolonged abstinence may worsen existing mental health problems; the NoFap community has been linked by scholars to manosphere ideas.

quick.overview:
This practice covers avoiding pornography, masturbation and other highly stimulating habits, with the aim of improving focus, confidence, attractiveness or mood. Communities such as NoFap and the 'dopamine fasting' trend frame it as resetting the brain's reward system.

In looksmaxxing circles, abstaining is often listed as a free self-improvement step alongside fitness and skincare. Proponents describe benefits such as willpower and confidence, while researchers report little supporting evidence.
quick.mechanism: Proponents say removing high-stimulation activities reduces impulsive behaviour and restores sensitivity to ordinary rewards. The psychologist who developed dopamine fasting, Cameron Sepah, has said the aim is to reduce impulsive behaviours rather than literally lower dopamine. Critics note that dopamine is vital and that avoiding a stimulus does not reset it.
quick.risks: Surveys found members' mental health problems were more plausibly linked to underlying disorders than to abstinence, and some researchers argue prolonged abstinence may worsen distress. Extreme versions such as sensory deprivation are criticised by clinicians. DSM-5-TR does not recognise porn addiction.

lead: Dopamine and porn avoidance refers to abstaining from pornography, masturbation and other stimulating behaviours in order to improve self-control, mood or perceived attractiveness. Two overlapping movements are involved: NoFap, an online community founded in June 2011 by Alexander Rhodes after a Reddit thread, and dopamine fasting, developed by psychologist Cameron Sepah as a cognitive behavioural tool [1][2].

Proponents describe benefits such as better relationships, willpower, self-improvement and so-called superpowers; Wikipedia reports the most prominent claimed benefits lack supporting evidence and that experts describe many NoFap views as simplistic or unsupported [1]. Regarding dopamine fasting, neuroscientists have criticised the idea of a dopamine 'reset', and Sepah says the goal is reducing impulsive behaviours rather than literally lowering dopamine [2].
infobox: Porn addiction not recognised in DSM-5-TR

paras: NoFap began as a subreddit in 2011 after a thread about a 2003 study claiming testosterone rose after seven days of abstinence; that study was retracted in 2021 [1]. Rhodes later built NoFap.com, which reports about 1.2 million users as of August 2025 [1]. Dopamine fasting originated with California psychologist Cameron Sepah as a CBT-based approach to impulsive behaviours and is often described as a Silicon Valley trend [2].

NoFap members cite improved relationships, willpower and mental clarity; the stated aim is reportedly reducing porn use and improving sexual health, and goals vary among members [1]. Dopamine fasting proponents say it builds self-discipline, with versions ranging from avoiding online technology to broader abstention [2].

A 2020 study found motivation to abstain was linked to viewing masturbation as unhealthy, religiosity, conservatism and lower trust in science, and a 2021 qualitative study found that framing abstinence around relapse appeared to sustain distress [1]. A 2023 preregistered survey by Prause and Binnie reported that members' mental health problems were more plausibly linked to underlying disorders than abstinence [1]. Psychologist David Ley and therapist Paula Hall say there is little medical evidence for claimed physical benefits [1]. The DSM-5-TR does not recognise porn addiction, and ICD-11 classifies compulsive sexual behaviour as an impulse control disorder [1].

On dopamine fasting, Peter Grinspoon called Sepah's work sensible but not groundbreaking, while neuroscientist Ciara McCabe disputes the idea of resetting the brain by avoiding dopamine triggers [2]. A 2022 paper in Lifestyle Medicine considered whether it is maladaptive or misunderstood [2].

No controlled clinical trials of porn or dopamine avoidance as a looksmaxxing or appearance intervention were found. Related observational and survey research on NoFap members and screen-time impulsivity exists [1][2].

Journalists and researchers have criticised some forum content as misogynistic and scholars have linked the community to the manosphere; Rhodes has also been involved in litigation against researchers [1].

timeline.event: NoFap founded as a subreddit by Alexander Rhodes [1].
The 2003 study that inspired NoFap is retracted [1].
Prause and Binnie survey reports on NoFap members' mental health [1].

lore.intro: Abstaining from porn and stimulation is commonly mentioned in looksmaxxing communities as part of broader self-improvement, and Wikipedia describes NoFap proponents' claims [1].

claims.claim: Abstaining resets dopamine and increases confidence, focus and attractiveness
claims.believers: Proponents cite willpower, better relationships and self-improvement [1].
claims.experts: Researchers say the claimed benefits lack supporting evidence and that dopamine cannot be reset by avoiding stimuli [1][2].

claims.believers: A Reddit thread about a 2003 study claimed a testosterone spike after seven days [1].
